events.label: Barker's Panorama
events.description: Robert Barker patents 'Apparatus for Exhibiting Pictures' and in 1788 exhibits the world's first full-circle panorama, a 360-degree view of Edinburgh from Calton Hill, in a purpose-built rotunda. Viewers stand on a raised central platform with sightlines controlled top and bottom so they cannot see where the painting ends. The first engineered apparatus built specifically to surround the visual field and blur where the image stops and reality begins — the starting point of a 190-year project of visual-immersion engineering that runs through Cinerama and into this pool's existing milestones.

outcomes.label: Panorama Becomes Mechanized
outcomes.description: Barker or an early follower mechanizes the panorama — a moving canvas, mechanical lighting or weather effects — decades before Daguerre's diorama introduces animation, collapsing the panorama/diorama distinction into a single continuous invention.
outcomes.requirement: Engineering investment in moving-canvas or mechanical-effects infrastructure within Barker's own rotunda business
outcomes.rationale: Provisional causal conversion of the legacy branch alternative. The narrative premise, requirement, and consequences are inherited; typed effects, influences, and six-axis values are preliminary judgments pending review.

influences.rationale: Mechanized panorama makes temporal scenic effects more likely to develop within the same lineage.

narrativeConsequences: The diorama's defining innovation (animated light and time-of-day effects) arrives decades earlier and is credited to Barker's tradition rather than treated as Daguerre's separate invention
The panorama-diorama lineage merges into one continuous project rather than splintering into two named media
Static panorama painting loses its status as the format's original, 'pure' form

events.label: Daguerre's Diorama
events.description: Louis Daguerre, working in the panorama tradition, opens the Diorama in Paris: large-scale paintings animated from behind the screen with shifting light to simulate the passage of time — dawn breaking, weather changing. Still purely visual and purely passive, but a genuine ancestor of both cinema and theatrical special effects, and the first entry in this pool to add temporal change to an otherwise static immersive image.

events.label: Wheatstone's Reflecting Stereoscope
events.description: Charles Wheatstone demonstrates that presenting each eye with a slightly different 2D image produces a compelling illusion of 3D depth. Establishes stereopsis as the primary technology for visual immersion. Begins a 190-year project of visual-depth enhancement.

outcomes.label: Documented historical path
outcomes.description: The documented historical development occurs as described in the milestone record.

events.label: Holmes's Handheld Stereoscope
events.description: Oliver Wendell Holmes designs a cheap simplified handheld stereoscope. The fork concerns whether he leaves the design open or patents and licenses it.

outcomes.label: Holmes leaves the design open
outcomes.description: Holmes deliberately leaves the simplified design unpatented, allowing inexpensive manufacture and rapid domestic adoption.
outcomes.rationale: The milestone's canonical description directly documents the open design and resulting mass adoption.
narrativeConsequences: Stereoview cards become familiar middle-class domestic media.
The medium establishes an early precedent for diffusion through openness rather than licensing.

outcomes.label: Holmes patents and licenses the design
outcomes.description: Holmes patents the simplified stereoscope and licenses it for a fee, prioritizing commercial return over rapid diffusion.
outcomes.requirement: Holmes or Joseph Bates decides the design's commercial value outweighs popular-science advocacy.
outcomes.rationale: Patent ownership is a direct effect; slower mass culture is modeled as reduced probability rather than an absolute prohibition.

influences.rationale: Licensing and higher prices delay broad adoption without making it impossible.

narrativeConsequences: Stereoscopic viewing remains an upper-middle-class practice for longer.
A licensing model becomes a visible precedent for later immersive-media ownership.

events.label: Stereoview Mass Culture Forms
events.description: Manufacturing, card publishing, and domestic adoption make stereoscopic viewing a normalized mass-market medium.

outcomes.label: Mass stereoview culture forms
outcomes.description: Stereoview production and circulation become broad enough to establish a durable domestic medium.
outcomes.requirement: Sufficient manufacturing and publishing capacity develops before the event window closes.
outcomes.rationale: This derived event makes delayed-but-still-possible adoption representable after either Holmes outcome.
narrativeConsequences: A shared visual vocabulary of travel, news, and domestic scenes develops around stereoview cards.

events.label: Ducos du Hauron's Anaglyph Patent
events.description: French scientist Louis Ducos du Hauron patents the anaglyph: separating an image into two color channels, viewed through correspondingly colored glasses, to reproduce stereo depth in a single printed or projected image. The technical basis for every red-green 3D film this pool's later 1922-1955 entries depend on.

events.label: Edison's Kinetoscope
events.description: William K. L. Dickson, working for Edison, completes the Kinetoscope: a peephole viewing cabinet that lets one person at a time watch a short looping film by cranking and peering in. First commercial exhibition April 1894, New York. Solitary, private, coin-operated. No projection, no shared audience, no screen.

outcomes.label: Documented historical path
outcomes.description: The documented historical development occurs as described in the milestone record.
outcomes.rationale: Canonical control outcome copied from the documented legacy milestone; its six-axis delta is a provisional translation of the legacy four-axis vector plus description-based accessibility, openness, and institutionalization judgments.

events.label: Lumière Cinématographe Exhibition Fork
events.description: Projected moving pictures become technically practical; the fork determines whether collective projection or Edison's private peephole model becomes commercially dominant.

outcomes.label: Collective theatrical projection prevails
outcomes.description: The Lumières secure paying audiences and cinema develops around projection to a shared public in darkened rooms.
outcomes.rationale: The collective exhibition model is the canonical historical outcome described by the milestone.
narrativeConsequences: Cinema becomes a shared public ritual rather than an individual cabinet experience.

outcomes.label: Private peephole exhibition prevails
outcomes.description: Patent enforcement or exhibition failure leaves the solitary coin-operated peephole model commercially dominant.
outcomes.requirement: Stronger Edison patent enforcement in Europe, or failure of the Lumières' Paris exhibition to draw paying crowds.
outcomes.rationale: The dominant social and venue forms are direct effects; the eventual cultural meaning remains narrative rather than hard state.
narrativeConsequences: Moving images develop socially like arcade cabinets or later headsets rather than theatrical cinema.
Any later collective cinema must emerge through a different event rather than being silently assumed.

events.label: Kinetoscope Parlors Become the Dominant Industry
events.description: Private coin-operated cabinets develop into the durable commercial system for moving-image exhibition.

outcomes.label: The parlor industry forms
outcomes.description: Investment and distribution consolidate around private cabinet venues.
outcomes.rationale: This event exists to make the Lumière counterfactual's immediate successor explicit and testable.
narrativeConsequences: Commercial moving-image culture standardizes around short, private, coin-operated encounters.

events.label: Hale's Tours of the World
events.description: Movie houses built as full-scale replica train carriages, seating up to 72 passengers, with front-of-train footage projected at one end, steam-whistle and wheel sound effects, fans blowing bursts of wind from the rear, and painted scenery rolling past the side windows. First exhibited Kansas City, May 1905; 500 US locations at its 1907 peak. A full multisensory, kinesthetic cinema experience fifty years before Sensorama, and structurally its closest ancestor in this pool.

outcomes.label: Documented historical path
outcomes.description: The documented historical development occurs as described in the milestone record.
outcomes.rationale: Canonical control outcome copied from the documented legacy milestone; its six-axis delta is a provisional translation of the legacy four-axis vector plus description-based accessibility, openness, and institutionalization judgments.

outcomes.label: Hales Tours Becomes Dominant Exhibition Model
outcomes.description: Rather than a five-year novelty fading by 1910, Hale's Tours' multisensory, kinesthetic exhibition format becomes the default template for movie-house construction, and fixed-seat flat-screen theaters develop as the minority format instead.
outcomes.requirement: Continued investor confidence and content variety (not just train footage) sustaining audience interest past its historical novelty period
outcomes.rationale: Provisional causal conversion of the legacy branch alternative. The narrative premise, requirement, and consequences are inherited; typed effects, influences, and six-axis values are preliminary judgments pending review.

influences.rationale: A durable multisensory cinema industry gives Heilig an established commercial lineage to extend.
Existing multisensory venues increase support for a Sensorama-class system.
A dominant kinesthetic theater model makes the Experience Theater legible to investors.

narrativeConsequences: The Heilig lineage's founding claim — that cinema must address the whole body, not just the eyes — has thirty years of commercial proof-of-concept before Heilig even publishes 'El Cine del Futuro' in 1955
Sensorama (1962) and the Experience Theater proposal (1964) read as continuations of an established commercial tradition rather than isolated inventions rejected by institutions
Cinema architecture and exhibitor economics through the mid-twentieth century are built around motion, wind, and sound infrastructure rather than optics and screen size alone

events.label: Shared Theatrical Cinema Consolidates
events.description: Projection, distribution, and purpose-built theaters consolidate collective cinema into a durable institution.

outcomes.label: The theater industry forms
outcomes.description: Shared projection becomes embedded in a durable theater and distribution system.
outcomes.rationale: This is a compact derived representation of the canonical collective-cinema lineage.
narrativeConsequences: Cinema architecture and distribution assume a shared audience as their default unit.

events.label: The Power of Love
events.description: The first 3D feature film, exhibited in anaglyph red/green at the Ambassador Hotel Theater in Los Angeles. Commercially unsuccessful — color balance is difficult to maintain and audiences find the glasses uncomfortable — and 3D filmmaking remains largely experimental for the next three decades rather than becoming a normalized part of Hollywood production.

outcomes.label: Documented historical path
outcomes.description: The documented historical development occurs as described in the milestone record.
outcomes.rationale: Canonical control outcome copied from the documented legacy milestone; its six-axis delta is a provisional translation of the legacy four-axis vector plus description-based accessibility, openness, and institutionalization judgments.

outcomes.label: Power Of Love Succeeds Commercially
outcomes.description: The Power of Love's anaglyph presentation solves its color-balance and eyestrain problems well enough to become a commercial hit, and 3D filmmaking becomes a normalized part of 1920s Hollywood rather than a curiosity abandoned until the 1950s.
outcomes.requirement: Better dye and filter stability for the red/green glasses, or immediate studio reinvestment following a strong opening
outcomes.rationale: Provisional causal conversion of the legacy branch alternative. The narrative premise, requirement, and consequences are inherited; typed effects, influences, and six-axis values are preliminary judgments pending review.

influences.rationale: Commercial anaglyph success increases investment in better stereoscopic projection.
An earlier normalized 3D industry makes the 1950s boom less likely to be a distinct first wave.

narrativeConsequences: This pool's existing '3D Film Golden Era' (1952-1955) happens thirty years early, and by the time it would historically have occurred it reads as a nostalgic revival rather than a first wave
Polarized 3D research (this pool's 1936-1939 entries) gets funded a decade earlier since anaglyph's commercial viability is already proven
Sound-film conversion (1926-1927) competes directly with an already-established 3D-film industry for capital and screen time, changing which innovation Hollywood prioritizes first

events.label: Vitaphone / Don Juan
events.description: Warner Bros. and Western Electric's Vitaphone sound-on-disc system debuts with Don Juan: no spoken dialogue, but nine synchronized discs of orchestral score and sound effects, recorded live and precisely matched to the reels. The first entry in this pool's cinema thread to add a genuinely new sensory channel — hearing — to what had been a purely visual medium.

events.label: The Jazz Singer
events.description: The first feature with synchronized spoken dialogue — only about a quarter of the film, but enough to end the silent era. Al Jolson's 'You ain't heard nothin' yet!' becomes the birth-cry of the talkies. Built on Vitaphone's fragile sound-on-disc system, which will lose the format war to sound-on-film (Movietone) within two years because discs kept drifting out of sync.

outcomes.label: Documented historical path
outcomes.description: The documented historical development occurs as described in the milestone record.
outcomes.rationale: Canonical control outcome copied from the documented legacy milestone; its six-axis delta is a provisional translation of the legacy four-axis vector plus description-based accessibility, openness, and institutionalization judgments.

outcomes.label: Sound On Film Wins First
outcomes.description: Fox's Movietone sound-on-film process reaches commercial maturity and wide rollout before Warner Bros' Vitaphone captures the 'first talkie' narrative with The Jazz Singer, so the industry standardizes on sound-on-film from the outset.
outcomes.requirement: Movietone's studio and distribution rollout outpacing Vitaphone's marketing and exhibition push in 1926-1927
outcomes.rationale: Provisional causal conversion of the legacy branch alternative. The narrative premise, requirement, and consequences are inherited; typed effects, influences, and six-axis values are preliminary judgments pending review.
narrativeConsequences: Theaters avoid several years of costly, unreliable disc-projector synchronization infrastructure entirely
The transition to sound is faster and cheaper industry-wide, since prints rather than fragile discs carry the audio track
Warner Bros. loses its historical claim to having 'invented' the talkies, changing which studio dominates the sound-conversion decade that follows

events.label: Polarized 3D Features
events.description: Beggars' Wedding (Italy, 1936) is the first sound stereoscopic feature and the first to use polarized filters rather than anaglyph color separation, solving the color-fringing and eyestrain problems that sank The Power of Love. In Tune With Tomorrow (1939) brings polarized 3D to American screens. Technically solves what anaglyph could not, but the Depression and the onset of WWII restrict industry investment, and 3D remains a marginal format until the pool's 1952 'Golden Era.'

outcomes.label: Documented historical path
outcomes.description: The documented historical development occurs as described in the milestone record.
outcomes.rationale: Canonical control outcome copied from the documented legacy milestone; its six-axis delta is a provisional translation of the legacy four-axis vector plus description-based accessibility, openness, and institutionalization judgments.

outcomes.label: Polarized 3D Arrives In Hollywood Immediately
outcomes.description: A major US studio invests in polarized-projection infrastructure immediately following In Tune With Tomorrow, rather than the format being sidelined by the Depression and the coming war.
outcomes.requirement: Studio capital available for exhibition-hardware investment in the late 1930s despite the economic and political climate
outcomes.rationale: Provisional causal conversion of the legacy branch alternative. The narrative premise, requirement, and consequences are inherited; typed effects, influences, and six-axis values are preliminary judgments pending review.

influences.rationale: Earlier studio adoption makes a separate 1950s breakthrough less likely.

narrativeConsequences: This pool's '3D Film Golden Era' (1952-1955) happens roughly fifteen years earlier and outside the postwar competition-with-television context that historically drove it
3D cinema's later reputation as 'a gimmick to compete with TV' never forms, since 3D predates mass television entirely in this branch
Heilig's 1955 manifesto, written as a critique of the historical 3D boom's collapse, either doesn't exist in this form or targets a completely different, earlier cultural moment

events.label: Fred Waller's Vitarama
events.description: Fred Waller's multi-projector panoramic system, shown at the 1939 World's Fair, uses several synchronized projectors and a curved screen to fill a wide field of view — the direct technical ancestor of this pool's 1952 Cinerama entry, and part of a flurry of realism-enhancing cinema experiments running from the 1920s through the early 1940s.

events.label: 3D Film Golden Era
events.description: Hollywood's first 3D boom: Bwana Devil (1952), House of Wax (1953), Creature from the Black Lagoon (1954), Dial M for Murder (1954). Over 50 3D features produced. The precise cultural context in which Heilig writes 'El Cine del Futuro' — he is critiquing cinema at its most immersively ambitious, arguing stereopsis alone is not enough.

outcomes.label: Documented historical path
outcomes.description: The documented historical development occurs as described in the milestone record.
outcomes.rationale: Canonical control outcome copied from the documented legacy milestone; its six-axis delta is a provisional translation of the legacy four-axis vector plus description-based accessibility, openness, and institutionalization judgments.

outcomes.label: 3D Boom Sustains
outcomes.description: The 3D golden era does not collapse in 1955 — improved polaroid systems solve sync and eyestrain problems, and 3D becomes the permanent default of Hollywood cinema.
outcomes.requirement: Technical solutions to eyestrain and projector sync; continued studio investment
outcomes.rationale: Provisional causal conversion of the legacy branch alternative. The narrative premise, requirement, and consequences are inherited; typed effects, influences, and six-axis values are preliminary judgments pending review.

influences.rationale: A sustained visual 3D boom sharpens the occasion for Heilig’s multisensory critique.

narrativeConsequences: Visual-only stereoscopic presence becomes the established cinema grammar
Heilig's somatic alternative has even less traction
The VR paradigm that eventually develops is even more visually centered

events.label: Cinerama Exhibition Fork
events.description: Cinerama combines a curved 146-degree image with synchronized projection and stereo sound; the fork determines whether theaters pursue visual scale alone or install repeatable multisensory effects.

outcomes.label: Visual scale and surround sound remain the standard
outcomes.description: Cinerama succeeds as a large-screen, surround-sound spectacle without standardizing wind, vibration, or scent.
outcomes.rationale: The canonical system expanded image and sound but did not establish durable nonvisual theater infrastructure.
narrativeConsequences: Commercial immersion continues to mean a larger image and richer sound rather than an environment addressing the whole body.

outcomes.label: Cinerama standardizes multisensory theaters
outcomes.description: Cinerama venues add wind, vibration, and scent and make those systems part of repeatable theater construction.
outcomes.requirement: Exhibitors fund multisensory infrastructure to differentiate theaters from television.
outcomes.rationale: The installation directly changes venue infrastructure; later Sensorama success is made likelier, not guaranteed.

influences.rationale: A multisensory theater market makes Heilig's system easier for investors to recognize.

narrativeConsequences: Sensorama enters a market that already understands bodily effects as cinema infrastructure rather than novelty machinery.

events.label: El Cine del Futuro (Heilig's Manifesto)
events.description: Morton Heilig publishes 'El Cine del Futuro' in a Mexican film journal. Argues that cinema must address all five senses to produce genuine presence. Written as the 3D boom collapses — Heilig diagnoses why: visual-only immersion is insufficient. Predates Sutherland's 'Ultimate Display' by a decade.

outcomes.label: Documented historical path
outcomes.description: The documented historical development occurs as described in the milestone record.
outcomes.rationale: Canonical control outcome copied from the documented legacy milestone; its six-axis delta is a provisional translation of the legacy four-axis vector plus description-based accessibility, openness, and institutionalization judgments.

events.label: Heilig Telesphere Mask Patent
events.description: Heilig patents the Telesphere Mask — a head-mounted display for stereoscopic TV and film with stereo sound. Predates Sutherland's HMD by eight years. Unlike Sutherland's later HMD, it is designed for cinematic content rather than computer graphics, and is non-interactive.

outcomes.label: Documented historical path

outcomes.label: Telesphere Tv Licensing
outcomes.description: A television network licenses the Telesphere Mask for home stereo TV broadcasts, making Heilig the pioneer of consumer HMDs rather than Sutherland.
outcomes.requirement: TV industry interest in premium immersive content; manufacturing at scale
outcomes.rationale: Provisional causal conversion of the legacy branch alternative. The narrative premise, requirement, and consequences are inherited; typed effects, influences, and six-axis values are preliminary judgments pending review.

influences.rationale: An established home-headset lineage makes later consumer VR adoption more likely.

narrativeConsequences: HMD as consumer entertainment device enters homes in the 1960s
Development pressure on lightweight, comfortable HMD design begins two decades earlier
The HMD paradigm develops from cinematic content tradition, not CGI

events.label: Sensorama Funding Fork
events.description: Morton Heilig completes a functioning multisensory cabinet combining stereo film, sound, vibration, wind, and smell; the fork determines whether any institution carries it beyond a prototype.

outcomes.label: No patron carries Sensorama forward
outcomes.description: Heilig fails to secure institutional or commercial backing, leaving Sensorama as an isolated prototype.
outcomes.rationale: Institutional failure despite a working prototype is the canonical milestone outcome.
narrativeConsequences: The somatic lineage survives as an idea without a durable organization or market.

outcomes.label: Private investors build a Sensorama arcade chain
outcomes.description: Private investors treat Sensorama as a premium amusement and fund a small network of commercial installations.
outcomes.requirement: An amusement or exhibition investor accepts the machine's maintenance costs and funds repeatable content production.
outcomes.rationale: Commercial backing is direct; eventual mass adoption remains unasserted.
narrativeConsequences: Somatic immersion develops through amusement economics and repeat customers rather than research procurement.

outcomes.label: DARPA funds somatic interface research
outcomes.description: Defense research funding adopts Sensorama's multisensory approach for simulation and training.
outcomes.requirement: A defense research sponsor treats wind, vibration, and smell as useful simulation channels rather than theatrical embellishments.
outcomes.rationale: The institutional home and research program are direct within the counterfactual; downstream consumer adoption is not encoded as certain.
narrativeConsequences: Somatic VR gains durable laboratories and procurement but develops under secrecy and training requirements.
Consumer uses may arrive later through technology transfer rather than direct entertainment investment.

events.label: Spacewar!
events.description: Martin Graetz, Wayne Witanen, and Steve Russell create Spacewar! at MIT — the first widely influential interactive computer game. Visual, two-player, competitive. Runs on a PDP-1 at MIT, the same institution and year as Sensorama, but in a completely different paradigm: interactive, computational, visual.

outcomes.label: Documented historical path
outcomes.description: The documented historical development occurs as described in the milestone record.
outcomes.rationale: Canonical control outcome copied from the documented legacy milestone; its six-axis delta is a provisional translation of the legacy four-axis vector plus description-based accessibility, openness, and institutionalization judgments.

events.label: BEFLIX (Bell Labs Computer Animation)
events.description: Ken Knowlton, an engineer at Bell Labs, builds BEFLIX ('Bell Flicks') on an IBM 7090 mainframe with a Stromberg-Carlson SC4020 microfilm recorder — a FORTRAN/assembly system of graphic primitives (draw line, copy region, fill area, zoom) for producing raster computer animation. Engineers building batch-processed, algorithmic imagery, but naming and organizing it entirely around cinematic vocabulary: frames, scenes, cuts. Knowlton later collaborates with artist Stan VanDerBeek on the Poemfields films (1966-1969), pulling the work toward the art world even as Sutherland's Sketchpad (also 1963) and subsequent HMD research proceed on a nominally separate, MIT/Harvard-based engineering track in the same small, cross-aware community of early computer-graphics researchers.

outcomes.label: Documented historical path
outcomes.description: The documented historical development occurs as described in the milestone record.
outcomes.rationale: Canonical control outcome copied from the documented legacy milestone; its six-axis delta is a provisional translation of the legacy four-axis vector plus description-based accessibility, openness, and institutionalization judgments.

outcomes.label: Beflix Sutherland Convergence
outcomes.description: Sutherland, aware of Bell Labs' work, directly incorporates BEFLIX's frame/scene/cut vocabulary and graphic-primitive approach into his own graphics research, rather than the two tracks staying institutionally separate.
outcomes.requirement: Institutional cross-pollination between Bell Labs and MIT/Harvard's graphics programs — a shared conference, joint proposal, or personnel exchange

influences.rationale: Direct exchange links cinematic computation to Sutherland’s interactive-display program.
A unified cinematic and interactive graphics field makes the later Hollywood bridge more likely.

narrativeConsequences: The Sutherland lineage of computer graphics explicitly inherits cinematic editing vocabulary rather than developing a separate engineering vocabulary of primitives and transforms
Real-time interactive graphics and algorithmic/generative animation develop as a single hybrid discipline rather than splitting into separate fields for decades
The convergence of cinema and games/VR, which historically takes until machinima and virtual production in the 1990s-2000s, happens as early as the 1960s

outcomes.label: Beflix Becomes Industry Standard
outcomes.description: Rather than remaining mostly an internal Bell Labs research and art tool, BEFLIX's graphic-primitive technique is published or licensed widely enough to become an early de facto standard for computer-generated visual effects in film and television.
outcomes.requirement: AT&T (barred as a regulated monopoly from directly competing in consumer computing) choosing to publish the technique broadly, or an outside studio adopting it independently
outcomes.rationale: Provisional causal conversion of the legacy branch alternative. The narrative premise, requirement, and consequences are inherited; typed effects, influences, and six-axis values are preliminary judgments pending review.

A mature production lineage increases the chance of a fully computer-animated feature.

narrativeConsequences: Computer-generated imagery enters commercial film and television production a decade or more before Tron (1982)
The 'graphic primitives' vocabulary, not the frame/scene/cut cinematic vocabulary, becomes the computer graphics industry's dominant technical language earlier
Bell Labs, rather than Lucasfilm/Pixar, becomes remembered as the seminal computer-animation studio

events.label: Defense-Funded Somatic Interface Program
events.description: A durable research program develops multisensory simulation interfaces for training and mission rehearsal.

outcomes.label: The defense research program forms
outcomes.description: Funding, laboratories, and personnel establish multisensory interfaces as an ongoing defense research field.
outcomes.rationale: This is the immediate institutional consequence of the authored DARPA alternative, not a claim that consumer success follows.
narrativeConsequences: A generation of researchers treats bodily sensation as a technical simulation problem.
Somatic interfaces gain continuity at the cost of secrecy and limited civilian access.

events.label: Sensorama Arcade Network Forms
events.description: Commercial operators standardize Sensorama installations, maintenance, and repeatable content across multiple venues.

outcomes.label: The arcade network forms
outcomes.description: A small but durable commercial network establishes Sensorama as a repeatable paid experience.
outcomes.rationale: This is the direct successor implied by the authored arcade-chain alternative.
narrativeConsequences: Full-body sensory installations become a known commercial category rather than a single inventor's artifact.

events.label: Heilig Experience Theater Proposal
events.description: Heilig proposes a full-scale multisensory theater — a room-sized Sensorama for audiences. Rejected by investors and institutions. The failure was not technical but institutional: no capital, no research backing, no corporate champion. This is the moment the Heilig lineage effectively loses its chance at development.

events.label: The Ultimate Display (Sutherland)
events.description: Ivan Sutherland publishes 'The Ultimate Display' at IFIP. Imagines a computer display as a room in which the computer can control the existence of matter — presence through total visual illusion. The foundational imaginative blueprint for visual VR. Completely ignores smell, touch, taste.

events.label: Sword of Damocles Research Fork
events.description: Ivan Sutherland's ceiling-mounted, head-tracked display establishes computer-generated head-mounted VR; the fork determines whether funding remains visual-first or supports a parallel somatic program.

outcomes.label: The visual HMD track dominates
outcomes.description: Research treats head tracking and computer graphics as VR's central problems while bodily feedback remains peripheral.
outcomes.rationale: The milestone directly establishes the visual-first HMD paradigm followed by later VR programs.
narrativeConsequences: For decades, progress in VR is measured primarily through display fidelity, tracking, and graphics.

outcomes.label: A parallel somatic track receives equal funding
outcomes.description: Defense research funds haptic and bodily simulation alongside Sutherland's visual display work as one coordinated immersive-environment program.
outcomes.requirement: Training sponsors treat touch and bodily cues as core simulation requirements rather than optional theatrical effects.
outcomes.rationale: The branch is adapted directly from the legacy milestone; it establishes research capacity but not consumer adoption.

influences.rationale: A continuous somatic research community makes commercial glove work easier to sustain.

narrativeConsequences: The headset and the haptic interface develop as coequal definitions of VR rather than as core device and accessory.

events.label: Videoplace Commercialization Fork
events.description: Myron Krueger's camera-based Videoplace puts unencumbered bodies into a shared responsive graphic space; the fork determines whether it remains arts research or becomes an entertainment interface.

outcomes.label: Videoplace remains an arts-research lineage
outcomes.description: Museums and arts grants sustain Videoplace as influential research without creating a mass commercial interface.
outcomes.rationale: The canonical event was publicly demonstrated and institutionally supported through arts funding, but not mass-commercialized.
narrativeConsequences: Room-based bodily interaction remains a powerful alternative idea without displacing the headset in the commercial imagination.

outcomes.label: Videoplace becomes a commercial entertainment platform
outcomes.description: An arcade or toy company licenses Videoplace and makes camera-based full-body interaction a familiar public interface.
outcomes.requirement: A commercial investor accepts the processing and installation costs of Krueger's prototype.
outcomes.rationale: The branch is adapted from the legacy milestone and records commercial interface adoption without assuming universal dominance.

influences.rationale: A commercial full-body lineage gives later motion gaming an established market vocabulary.

narrativeConsequences: Consumers encounter virtual environments first as shared rooms that read their bodies, not as images sealed inside headsets.

events.label: Lucasfilm Computer Division Founded
events.description: George Lucas recruits Ed Catmull — a direct PhD student of Ivan Sutherland at the University of Utah's DARPA-funded computer graphics program, alongside fellow students Jim Clark and Alan Kay — to head a new Computer Division at Lucasfilm, tasked with bringing digital film editing, digital sound, and computer graphics into commercial filmmaking. The Sutherland engineering lineage, incubated inside defense-funded academic research, pivots explicitly toward Hollywood entertainment for the first time.

outcomes.description: Catmull, instead of joining Lucasfilm, takes an academic or defense-contractor position continuing the DARPA-funded simulation/graphics work directly — flight simulation, NASA-adjacent work — rather than pivoting to commercial filmmaking.
outcomes.requirement: No entertainment-industry recruiter makes an attractive offer, or Catmull's own interests stay closer to the simulation and training applications his Utah cohort was funded to pursue

Computer-generated imagery in commercial film is delayed by a decade or more, or is pioneered by a different, less Utah-DARPA-descended team
Steve Jobs never has a computer-graphics division to acquire in 1986; Pixar in its historical form does not exist

events.label: NASA VIEW Program
events.description: NASA Ames develops the Virtual Interface Environment Workstation (VIEW) — an HMD with DataGlove for telepresence and simulation. First major institutional application of visual VR after Sutherland. Establishes VR as a serious research and operational tool.

outcomes.description: NASA VIEW program includes a parallel multisensory track — developing full-body haptic suits and olfactory interfaces alongside the visual HMD.
outcomes.requirement: NASA interest in realistic simulation of planetary environments for astronaut training

Institutional body-interface research raises the later visibility of motion control.

events.label: VPL Product-Priority Fork
events.description: VPL Research commercializes both the EyePhone HMD and DataGlove; the fork determines which becomes the company's defining product and the public emblem of VR.

outcomes.label: The EyePhone HMD defines commercial VR
outcomes.description: VPL's head-mounted display becomes the recognizable image of VR while the DataGlove remains an expensive supporting interface.
outcomes.rationale: The visual HMD became the durable public icon even though VPL also advanced gesture input.
narrativeConsequences: The headset becomes visual shorthand for virtual reality in laboratories, journalism, and popular culture.

outcomes.label: The DataGlove becomes VPL's defining platform
outcomes.description: VPL prioritizes gesture, touch, and the DataGlove over display fidelity and builds its markets around bodily control.
outcomes.requirement: Investors or medical and training customers value haptic precision more than a more convincing visual display.
outcomes.rationale: The legacy branch changes product priority, not the existence of either device.

influences.rationale: A haptic-first commercial vocabulary slightly reduces the pull of a visual-first revival without preventing it.

narrativeConsequences: Touch and gesture, rather than visual enclosure, become the feature by which the public judges a virtual environment.

events.label: Nintendo Power Glove
events.description: Nintendo and Mattel release the Power Glove — a consumer gesture/haptic controller for the NES. Fails commercially (poor tracking accuracy, few compatible games). Becomes culturally iconic as a failed future. The first mass-market attempt to make gesture/body interface the gaming paradigm.

outcomes.requirement: Better accelerometer technology; Nintendo commitment to game development for the format

The somatic paradigm in gaming has a 10-year head start

events.label: Osmose (Char Davies)
events.description: Painter-turned-Softimage-VP Char Davies debuts Osmose at the Musée d'art contemporain de Montréal: a stereoscopic HMD and biometric vest whose only interface is breath and balance — exhaling sinks the immersant through a layered virtual landscape, inhaling lifts them. Built on the same HMD hardware lineage as Sutherland and VPL's research systems, but explicitly conceived by Davies as a corrective to what she called VR's masculine, militarized, conquest-oriented design language — replacing joysticks and gloves with the most involuntary, unconquerable interface available.

outcomes.label: Osmose Influences Consumer Vr
outcomes.description: Osmose's breath/balance interface research is licensed or adapted by a VR hardware company as an input method alongside or instead of handheld controllers, rather than remaining a singular fine-art installation.
outcomes.requirement: A VR hardware company investing in biometric sensing for consumer hardware rather than treating it as a one-off art-world experiment
outcomes.rationale: Provisional causal conversion of the legacy branch alternative. The narrative premise, requirement, and consequences are inherited; typed effects, influences, and six-axis values are preliminary judgments pending review.

narrativeConsequences: Consumer VR from the late 1990s onward includes biometric, involuntary-bodily input as a standard alongside hand controllers, rather than these appearing decades later in wellness-oriented VR
VR's popular design language incorporates Davies's explicit critique of conquest/mastery interaction models earlier and more broadly
Later controller-and-gesture-based headsets in this pool exist in a market that already expects a biometric option, changing their design briefs

events.label: Toy Story / Pixar's Fully Computer-Animated Feature
events.description: Sixteen years after Lucasfilm's Computer Division was founded, and nine years after Steve Jobs spun it off as Pixar (1986), Pixar releases Toy Story — the first entirely computer-animated feature film, roughly 800,000 render-hours, no traditional cel animation at any stage. A direct institutional and personal descendant of Sutherland's Sketchpad and the Utah DARPA program reaches mass-market Hollywood entertainment. Like every milestone in this Sutherland-descended thread, it is purely audiovisual — no haptic, olfactory, or other sensory channel is addressed, however emotionally 'present' the animated characters are made to feel.

outcomes.label: Cg Animation Stays Hybrid
outcomes.description: Full CG animation proves commercially unconvincing at feature length in 1995 — rendering costs, character believability — and the industry instead settles for another decade on a hybrid model, CG effects and sequences embedded within traditionally animated or live-action films, rather than an all-CG feature.
outcomes.requirement: Toy Story's character animation or box-office reception falling short of what made it convincing historically, or Disney hedging with a hybrid release strategy

narrativeConsequences: Fully computer-animated features arrive in the 2000s rather than 1995, delaying the reallocation of Hollywood animation labor and capital toward CG studios by a decade
Pixar itself, without Toy Story's proof-of-concept success, is acquired, absorbed, or wound down rather than becoming an independent powerhouse
Traditional 2D animation studios retain market and cultural dominance for longer, changing the competitive landscape Disney's own animation division operates in through the 1990s-2000s

events.label: Wii Somatic-Legacy Fork
events.description: The Wii makes bodily motion a mass-market game interface; the fork determines whether Nintendo leaves that success at the television, turns it into VR hardware, or redirects research funding.

outcomes.label: Motion gaming remains screen-based
outcomes.description: The Wii proves mass demand for bodily control but Nintendo does not turn it into an immersive headset or multisensory platform.
outcomes.rationale: The console achieved mass motion interaction without becoming VR hardware.
narrativeConsequences: Mass bodily interaction and headset VR remain separate product categories as Oculus approaches.

outcomes.label: Nintendo builds motion-first consumer VR
outcomes.description: Nintendo pairs Wii-scale bodily control with an affordable headset and defines consumer VR through movement before Oculus.
outcomes.requirement: Nintendo treats immersive hardware as the next use of its motion-interface advantage and accepts the display risks.
outcomes.rationale: The branch is adapted from the legacy milestone and asserts an early product category, not permanent market victory.
narrativeConsequences: Oculus enters a market where consumers already expect a virtual world to begin with movement rather than display fidelity.

outcomes.label: Wii success redirects VR research toward the body
outcomes.description: Funders treat the Wii as proof of the somatic paradigm and support haptics and multisensory presence before consumer headsets return.
outcomes.requirement: Research institutions read motion gaming as evidence for immersive-interface priorities rather than only console design.
outcomes.rationale: The branch follows the legacy milestone's second alternative and records research capacity rather than a finished product.
narrativeConsequences: The haptic suit, not merely the headset display, becomes the consumer-VR research problem of the following decade.

events.label: Oculus Consumer-VR Fork
events.description: Cheap smartphone displays and inertial sensors make consumer headsets plausible again; the fork determines whether visual VR returns alone or beside a funded haptic platform.

outcomes.label: The visual Rift leads the revival
outcomes.description: Oculus makes low-latency visual presence the center of the consumer VR revival, with bodily feedback treated as a later accessory problem.
outcomes.rationale: The canonical Kickstarter and product roadmap centered the headset and its visual tracking problem.
narrativeConsequences: A convincing, affordable view becomes the price of entry for the new consumer category.

outcomes.label: A haptic platform launches beside the Rift
outcomes.description: A parallel crowdfunding success establishes an affordable haptic platform alongside Oculus, making visual and somatic VR coequal consumer expectations.
outcomes.requirement: A credible hardware team converts post-Wii appetite for bodily play into a manufacturable haptic product.
outcomes.rationale: The branch is adapted from the legacy milestone; it establishes a competing platform without assuming which wins.
narrativeConsequences: Any acquirer of Oculus must decide whether to absorb, compete with, or interoperate with an established bodily interface.

events.label: John Carmack Joins Oculus as CTO
events.description: id Software's John Carmack — the engineer behind Doom and Quake's real-time 3D engines — resigns to join Oculus VR full-time as CTO after ZeniMax Media, id's parent company, declines to support Oculus. A second engineering lineage (real-time game-engine development) merges into the Sutherland-descended VR hardware track. ZeniMax later sues Oculus and Facebook for trade-secret misappropriation and wins a $500 million judgment.

events.label: Oculus Acquisition Fork
events.description: Oculus becomes valuable enough to acquire; the fork determines whether a social advertising platform or a gaming and hardware company becomes VR's principal corporate patron.

outcomes.label: Facebook acquires Oculus
outcomes.description: Facebook buys Oculus and makes social connection, platform scale, and engagement central to its institutional future.
outcomes.rationale: The acquisition and purchaser are canonical documented history.
narrativeConsequences: Consumer VR is pulled toward social-platform scale and away from the priorities of an independent gaming startup.

outcomes.label: A gaming or hardware company acquires Oculus
outcomes.description: Sony, Valve, Samsung, or a comparable hardware firm outbids Facebook and centers Oculus on games, devices, and hardware quality.
outcomes.requirement: A hardware company accepts the acquisition price or Facebook's board declines the purchase.
outcomes.rationale: The legacy branch identifies plausible alternative purchasers and directly changes institutional control.
narrativeConsequences: There is no Facebook VR division around which to build a company-wide metaverse identity in 2021.

events.label: Consumer VR Launch (Oculus CV1, HTC Vive, PSVR)
events.description: Three consumer VR headsets launch within months of each other. Visual VR at consumer price points. Room-scale tracking (Vive) is new; controllers are the interaction paradigm. The Sutherland visual-computational lineage reaches mass-market consumer deployment after 48 years.

events.description: Oculus founder Palmer Luckey is forced out of Facebook following revelation of his $10,000 donation to a pro-Trump group that ran a controversial anti-Clinton billboard. Facebook denies the departure was politically motivated. Founder-vs-corporate-parent friction, the same shape this pool's Silicon Valley theme captures later with Kalanick and Neumann.

events.label: Meta Rebrand Fork
events.description: Facebook must decide whether social VR remains one product line or becomes the identity and capital-allocation thesis of the whole company.

outcomes.label: Facebook becomes Meta
outcomes.description: The company renames itself Meta and makes the metaverse a company-defining investment thesis.
outcomes.rationale: The rebrand and strategic commitment are canonical documented history.
narrativeConsequences: The entire technology industry receives a highly visible signal that social VR is a platform-scale future.

outcomes.label: VR remains a bounded Facebook product line
outcomes.description: Facebook keeps its name and limits VR spending to a product division rather than staking its identity on the metaverse.
outcomes.requirement: Leadership or the board treats the metaverse thesis as too speculative for a company-wide commitment.
outcomes.rationale: The legacy alternative directly changes corporate commitment without asserting that VR disappears.
narrativeConsequences: No singular metaverse-craze moment gives the wider industry a shared object of imitation and backlash.

events.label: Reality Labs' Losses Mount, AI Pivot Begins
events.description: Reality Labs racks up close to $90 billion in cumulative operating losses since 2020. By late 2024, executives have quietly stopped saying 'metaverse' on earnings calls. Layoffs, VR studio closures, and spending cuts of up to 30% follow as resources shift toward AI. The craze visibly abating — not a single event but a multi-year deflation, the mirror image of the Meta rebrand's 2021 peak.

events.label: Apple Vision Pro
events.description: Apple launches the Vision Pro at $3,499 — ultra-high-fidelity visual display, spatial computing, eye and hand tracking, passthrough AR/MR. Repositioned as 'spatial computer,' not headset. The culmination of the Sutherland lineage as pure optical hardware. No somatic channels; purely optical presence. Arrives in the same year Meta's Reality Labs losses are mounting and a full two years before generative world models and a second Meta reversal on Horizon Worlds extend this pool's timeline further still.

events.label: Generative World-Model Fork
events.description: Genie-class systems generate interactive environments from prompts and images; the fork determines whether they remain research demonstrations or become a consumer VR content engine.

outcomes.label: World models remain research systems
outcomes.description: Generative interactive environments advance rapidly but remain research platforms rather than the primary way consumer VR content is made.
outcomes.rationale: Within the pilot's 2025 endpoint, the documented systems remain research demonstrations rather than deployed consumer VR engines.
narrativeConsequences: The environment becomes generative in the laboratory while consumer virtual worlds remain largely hand-authored.

outcomes.label: World models become a consumer VR engine
outcomes.description: A headset maker integrates a Genie-class model and lets users prompt responsive virtual environments instead of relying on hand-built 3D scenes.
outcomes.requirement: A hardware partner solves the latency and consistency problems well enough for an embodied consumer product.
outcomes.rationale: The legacy branch defines a direct product integration while leaving its ultimate adoption open.
narrativeConsequences: Authorship shifts from specialist 3D production toward prompting, and virtual worlds respond to users by being regenerated around them.

events.label: World Labs and Spatial Intelligence (Fei-Fei Li)
events.description: Fei-Fei Li — Stanford computer vision professor, architect of ImageNet, and co-director of Stanford's Human-Centered AI institute — raises $230 million in September 2024 to found World Labs, betting that 'spatial intelligence' is AI's next frontier after language. In November 2025 the company launches Marble, a commercial platform generating exportable 3D environments from text, image, or video prompts. A $1 billion follow-on round, with Autodesk investing $200 million and taking an advisory seat, signals that the incumbent 3D-content-creation industry sees world-generation as displacement, not supplement. Another Stanford-incubated venture, in the same institutional lineage as Terman's students decades earlier, but selling spatial generation rather than hardware.

events.label: Horizon Worlds Shutdown-Then-Reversal
events.description: In March 2026, Meta announces it is shutting down the VR version of Horizon Worlds as it shifts focus to AI — then reverses the decision within 48 hours after user backlash. The most recent dated event in this pool: the metaverse craze's whiplash coda, five years after the Meta rebrand and squarely in the middle of Reality Labs' sustained retreat. The reversal holds by a thread — user backlash, not a change of strategic heart, is what kept Horizon Worlds alive on VR, and nothing in Meta's public reasoning ruled out revisiting the shutdown later. Whether this reads as the end of 'the metaverse' or merely a contested, temporary pause is left for the story to decide, since this is the last dated event in the pool and nothing follows it to settle the question.
